About: a rolling wheel meets a step corner

Source

Concept
A rolling disc meets the sharp corner of a raised step in a brief sticking impact, then pivots about the corner. Whether it climbs, and at what launch speed, is the question the inquiry settles.
Model
rolls without slipping (ω = v/R); the strike is sticking, no bounce; the corner grip holds through the pivot
Serves
JEE / NCERT rigid-body rotation: moment of inertia, angular momentum about a point, impulsive torque, energy in an inelastic collision.
Inquiry
Which quantity survives the impact, how the spin just after compares with the spin just before, how the energy books balance across the strike, and how the threshold speed depends on the step height.
Misconception
Addressed in card 3: the student commits to a plausible energy-balance prediction, then launches the wheel at exactly that speed to test it.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealFive gated cards each commit a prediction before the answer-bearing readout or mgh line is unveiled.
Target the misconceptionCard 3 has the student launch the wheel at their own predicted threshold speed and watch what it does.
Invariant made visibleThe strike ledger tracks L about the corner alongside the energy bars, so the student sees for themselves which quantities the impact moves.
Operational numbersEvery readout is a kernel number from the single collision computation; the spoke's rate matches the ω readouts.
Stable, honest sceneFixed 1.2 m × 0.6 m frame, real SI units, slow-motion at the corner labelled explicitly.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Across the strike

The wheel rolls towards the step at 1.2 m s⁻¹ with the height set to 0.10 m. During the brief sticking impact at the corner, before predicting the outcome, decide which quantity is unchanged across the impact.

2 · Spin after sticking

The spoke lets you compare the spin just before and just after the impact. Before pressing go, predict how the angular speed just after the wheel sticks to the corner compares with the angular speed of rolling just before.

3 · Naive threshold

A student balances the rolling kinetic energy ¾mv² against mgh for the 0.10 m step and predicts a threshold speed of 1.14 m s⁻¹. Before launching the wheel at exactly that speed, predict what it does.

4 · Fraction vs speed

The readout shows the energy lost in the impact. Before trying a faster launch at the same step height, predict how the fraction of the kinetic energy lost in the collision changes as the launch speed is raised.

5 · Taller step

At height 0.10 m the threshold speed is 1.47 m s⁻¹. For a smooth ramp the needed speed would grow as √h, which predicts 1.80 m s⁻¹ at 0.15 m. Before moving the height slider to 0.15 m, predict the threshold there.

The Physics

Wheel meeting a step · what it is about, the physics behind it, and what every control does

A rolling wheel meets the sharp corner of a step. The whole question is decided in the instant it arrives — and two sliders set up that instant.

1What you'll work out

  • Which quantity survives the brief, violent impact at the corner — and which ones do not, however rigid the corner is.
  • How the wheel's spin just after the strike compares with its spin just before, and why that comparison is not the obvious one.
  • What speed it actually takes to get over a step — and why balancing the rolling energy against mgh gives the wrong answer.

JEE / NCERT Class 11 — rigid-body rotation, moment of inertia, angular momentum about a point, and impulsive torque.

2What this simulation shows

A uniform disc of mass m = 1 kg and radius R = 0.30 m rolls without slipping toward a step. The strike at the corner is a sticking impact — no bounce — and the corner keeps its grip while the wheel pivots about it. From there the wheel either makes it onto the step or falls back.

The moment to watch is the corner itself. Everything that decides the outcome happens in that instant, before the climb has even begun — which is why the painted spoke is there: it lets you compare the spin on either side of the strike.

The strike is over in an instant, and it is the whole problem. Everything the wheel needs to climb, it has to survive that instant with.

01

What survives the impact — and why that one thing?

The instant of contact: the wheel touches the ground and the corner at the same moment. Geometry computed from the sim's R = 0.30 m and h = 0.10 m.
  • The corner hits the wheel with a huge, brief force. It changes the momentum — so linear momentum is not conserved, and neither is kinetic energy.
  • But that force acts at the corner, so about that point its moment arm is zero and it exerts no torque. Angular momentum about the corner is therefore untouched.
  • Before the strike that angular momentum has two pieces: the wheel's own spin Icmω, plus its centre's momentum acting at a moment arm of R − h.
The two contributions, added. Note it is R − h, not R: the corner is already part-way up.
Why this one quantity and not the others — the same impulse that ruins p and K leaves L about the corner alone.
02

How much spin is left the instant after?

After the strike the wheel turns about the corner, not its own centre — so the parallel-axis moment of inertia is what matters.
Divide the conserved L by the new, larger moment of inertia. The bracket is the surviving fraction.
  • Conserving L does not mean conserving ω. The pivot moved from the centre to the corner, and I went up from ½mR² to 3/2 mR².
  • The same L divided by a bigger I gives a smaller ω: at the sim's defaults, 4.0000 rad s⁻¹ drops to 3.1111, a factor of 7/9.
  • The surviving fraction s = 1 − 2h/3R depends only on the step height. At h = 0.05 m you keep 8/9 of your spin; at h = 0.15 m only 2/3.
03

Where did the energy go?

The ledger at the sim's defaults. The green line is what the climb costs; the strike happens first.
Rolling kinetic energy is ¾mv², not ½mv² — half of the extra quarter is spin. After the strike, the same expression with s².
  • Energy is not conserved in a sticking impact. Scaling ω by s scales the energy by s²: at the defaults 1.0800 J becomes 0.6533 J, and 0.4267 J is simply gone into the corner.
  • That is 39.51% of the wheel's kinetic energy destroyed in an instant — before the climb has even started.
  • Judged before the strike, 1.0800 J looks comfortably more than the 0.9800 J the climb needs. Judged after, 0.6533 J is not enough. The wheel falls back.
04

Does a harder impact waste a bigger share?

The lost fraction, in closed form. Every symbol in it is geometry.
Both curves against step height, computed from the sim's kernel. Neither has v in it.
  • No. Both ω and the energy scale by fixed factors of s and s², and s has no v in it — so the fraction lost is the same at every launch speed.
  • A faster wheel loses more joules and the same percentage. Those are different statements, and the card is asking about the second.
  • The only way to change the fraction is to change the step height: 20.99% at h = 0.05 m, 39.51% at 0.10 m, 55.56% at 0.15 m.
05

So what speed does it actually take?

Energy after the strike against the climb, solved for v. The whole correction is the single factor 1/s.
Threshold speed against step height: the truth, the no-loss answer, and the √h rule. All three computed from the sim's kernel.
  • Balance after the strike, not before: ½Icornerωafter² ≥ mgh gives vmin = (1/s)·√(4gh/3).
  • At h = 0.10 m the no-loss answer is 1.1431 m s⁻¹ and the truth is 1.4697 — exactly 9/7 times bigger, because s = 7/9.
  • The threshold grows faster than √h: taller steps cost more to climb and destroy more spin on the way in. At h = 0.15 m the √h rule predicts 1.7999 and the answer is 2.1000.
06

The traps they'll set for you

  • "The collision is with a rigid corner, so energy is conserved." Rigid means no bouncing back, not no loss. A sticking impact is perfectly inelastic in the rotational sense and destroys 39.51% of the energy at the default step.
  • "Angular momentum is conserved, so the spin is unchanged." L is conserved; ω is not. The axis moved to the corner and I tripled, so ω had to drop.
  • "Momentum is conserved because the impact is brief." Brief is exactly what makes the corner's force enormous. Only the moment of that force vanishes — and only about the corner.
  • "Balance ¾mv² against mgh." That is the card-3 trap: it gives 1.1431 m s⁻¹, and the wheel launched at exactly that speed falls back. The balance has to be struck after the strike.
  • "A faster wheel wastes a bigger fraction." Same fraction, more joules. 1 − s² contains no v at all.
  • "Rolling kinetic energy is ½mv²." For a rolling disc it is ¾mv² — the spin carries a third of it.
07

Ninety-second self-test

Why is the moment arm R − h and not R?

The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the corner to the line of the centre's velocity. That velocity is horizontal at height R; the corner is at height h; so the line misses the corner by R − h. Using R would be the moment about a point on the ground, which is not the pivot.

What would happen to the surviving fraction if the step were as tall as the wheel's radius, h = R?

s = 1 − 2R/3R = 1/3, so only a third of the spin survives and 1 − s² = 8/9 of the energy is destroyed. The formula keeps working right up to h = R; beyond that the wheel would strike the face rather than the corner, and this model no longer applies.

The sim shows the wheel failing at 1.2 m s⁻¹ on the 0.10 m step. By what factor must you raise the speed to just clear it?

The threshold is 1.4697 m s⁻¹, so a factor 1.2247 — about 22% faster. Note that the energy needed goes as v², so that is a 50% increase in kinetic energy for a 22% increase in speed.

Is there any step height this wheel cannot clear, however fast you launch it?

Within this model, no — vmin = (1/s)√(4gh/3) is finite for every h < R, so enough speed always works. But the factor 1/s blows up as h approaches R, so the required speed climbs very steeply; and in reality the wheel would bounce or slip long before the sticking assumption held.
